content: Even at low viral loads, HIV transmission through shared drug injection equipment has been observed, though at low rates. However, no studies have specifically evaluated the risk of HIV transmission via shared injection equipment when the viral load is below 1000 copies/mL. In many settings, alternative technologies such as dried blood spots and point-of-care testing are used to expand access to viral load testing. While some technologies perform reliably at lower thresholds for treatment failure, others show significantly poorer sensitivity and specificity, often failing to exceed 90% accuracy. Wide confidence intervals in some studies highlight the need for further research to better understand the performance of these technologies. Experts emphasize the importance of distinguishing between viral suppression and treatment failure, which may require a change in therapy. The global shift toward dolutegravir (DTG)-based regimens should also be acknowledged. The treatment failure threshold remains at 1000 copies/mL, as determined by the Guideline Development Group. Adherence counseling is critical during antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation and throughout treatment, especially after elevated viral load results. Viral load results can motivate adherence and help achieve viral suppression. Clinicians, healthcare providers, and peer counselors must receive adequate training on ART, including transitioning to optimal regimens, managing treatment failure, switching therapies, and supporting adherence. For pregnant and breastfeeding women, point-of-care viral load testing enables faster clinical decision-making to prevent vertical transmission. Drug resistance rates are higher in infants, children, and adolescents compared to adults, making rapid results essential to prevent the development of resistance mutations and preserve future treatment options. Viral load testing at 34–36 weeks of gestation (or at delivery) is recommended to identify women at risk of treatment failure or perinatal transmission. If viral load exceeds 1000 copies/mL, enhanced postnatal prophylaxis for the infant and adherence counseling for the mother should be provided. For breastfeeding women, viral load testing should be conducted three months postpartum and every six months thereafter to detect viremia during the postnatal period. Point-of-care testing is particularly valuable for high-risk groups, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, infants, children, adolescents, and individuals with advanced HIV disease or suspected treatment failure. Point-of-care viral load testing offers several advantages, including faster results, fewer clinic visits, and improved clinical action following elevated viral loads. It also increases the likelihood of long-term viral suppression, retention in care, and transition to differentiated care for those with sustained suppression. However, challenges such as higher costs and limited test throughput must be addressed. Current technologies require plasma separation from whole blood, necessitating additional equipment and expertise. Research gaps remain, particularly regarding the clinical relevance of low-level viremia (50–1000 copies/mL) and its relationship to drug resistance mutations in DTG-based regimens. Further studies are needed to optimize treatment monitoring algorithms for pregnant and breastfeeding women and to evaluate the cost-effectiveness and feasibility of point-of-care testing in various settings. Efforts should focus on expanding access to high-quality diagnostic testing, integrating laboratory-based and point-of-care technologies, and strengthening diagnostic systems. Clear communication and collaboration with community groups are essential to support scale-up and trust in viral load testing. Prioritizing adherence interventions and retention in care will maximize the clinical impact of point-of-care testing and reduce delays in switching treatment when necessary.
